text:
Stieber c. Joseph Élie ltée

2009 QCCS 2498

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-06-000426-086

DATE:

MARCH 5, 2012

______________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

MR. JUSTICE MARK G. PEACOCK, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

ALBERT STIEBER
,

Petitioner

v.

JOSEPH ÉLIE LTÉE
,

Respondent

-And-

FONDS D'AIDE AUX RECOURS
COLLECTIFS
,

Mis En Cause

______________________________________________________________________

RE-RECTIFIED JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

Joseph Élie Ltée is an established distributor
of heating oil to residences and businesses in the Greater Montreal area.
Unfortunately and unbeknownst to Joseph Élie Ltée, certain unscrupulous third
party delivery companies with which it contracted had illegally tampered with
the gear-train in the flow meters on their trucks. These trucks were then used
to measure the quantity of heating oil delivered to the customer. As a result
of this tampering, customers were charged by Joseph Élie Ltée for more heating
oil than had been delivered.

[
2
]

The fraudulent tampering was
originally uncovered as a result of inspections undertaken by Measurements
Canada in the course of their inspections. The perpetrators of this fraudulent
activity were successfully prosecuted.

[
3
]

It was as a result of these overcharges that
these class action proceedings were brought against the distributor, Joseph Élie Ltée.

[
4
]

The class action was ultimately settled out of
court. The Court approved the authorization application and the settlement at
the same time: the Settlement Agreement was approved by Rectified Reasons for
Judgment by this Court dated May 29, 2009 (the "Rectified Reasons").

[
5
]

The Court is asked to re-rectify its Rectified
Reasons:

a)         by the Respondent, Joseph Élie Ltée; and

b)         by the Fonds d'aide aux recours collectifs ("the
Fonds"), each for different reasons;

Joseph Élie Ltée alleges miscalculations caused by inadvertent human
error. For itself, the Fonds asserted that it erred in accepting an amount less
than its statutory entitlement.

A-        Joseph Élie Ltée’s Claim for Rectification

[
6
]

Joseph Élie Ltée
alleges that the Total Indemnity to be distributed to its customers should have
been $3,570,488.03, in lieu of the Total Indemnity of $4,461,046.68, as noted
in paragraph 4.1.2 of the Settlement Agreement approved by the Rectified
Judgment of May 29, 2009.

[
7
]

The factual basis for Joseph
Élie Ltée’s Motion is contained in its Re-Amended Motion for Rectification of
Judgment (…) and for approval of the administration of the Settlement Agreement
as approved by this Honourable Court (art. 2, 20, 46, 475 and 1022 of the
Code
of Civil Procedure
.

[
8
]

The relevant paragraphs are:

"9. ln accordance
with Mr. Justice Peacock's judgment, the Respondent established a claims
process to reach and reimburse those Class Members who suffered a loss, all the
while keeping class counsel apprised of the progression of the process;

10. However, during the
process and while executing the judgement approving the Settlement Agreement,
the Respondent discovered that it had made errors in the Records, which formed
the basis of the Total and Net Indemnity set forth in the Settlement Agreement;

11. The Respondent
established the Total Indemnity by relying on a computer program which
correlated 1) the ratio of oil diverted per truck established by Measurement
Canada, 2) the period over which such diversion would have taken place, and 3)
the number of oil deliveries made to its customers from the diverted trucks;

12. It now appears that
the computer program used was mistakenly encoded in such a way that
duplicated
transactions appeared affecting certain customers (4065) amongst the 13 600
customers included in the final database
;

13. As a result of the
foregoing error, the amount of the Total and the Net Indemnity are greater than
the amounts for which Class Members were charged by the Respondent for
undelivered heating oil;

14. Indeed, after taking
out the few accounts already settled prior to the Settlement Agreement (2) and
those that should not be considered, like the accounts of the two carriers
involved and those of certain JEL's employees (13), the total number of clients
to which the Settlement Agreement and the judgement approving same applied was
13 232, for a total volume of oil diverted of 48 630 344.80 litres instead of
59 894 954.9 and the Total lndemnity should have been established at
$3,570,488.03 while the Net Indemnity should have been $3,268,195.08 the whole
as appears from a summary of various relevant amounts produced herewith as
Exhibit R-1;

15. As a result of the
foregoing error, the reliquat is greater than the unpaid and unclaimed portion
of the true amounts charged to Class members for undelivered heating oil;

.

.

.

18. Given the Total
Indemnity's overvaluation, the unpaid portion of the Net Indemnity that must be
donated is therefore over-valued by an amount of $804,017.40. It is only the
real unpaid portion remaining after the completion of the entire process of
indemnification of the Class Members in full compliance with the Settlement
Agreement that constitutes the "reliquat" to be donated to charities;

19. After the completion
of the process of indemnification, including the publication of the Final
Notices in both newspaper La Presse and The Gazette on September 11, 2010, as
authorized by this Court on July 23, 2010, in order to give Class Members a
final opportunity to make a claim (copies of which are produced herewith as
Exhibit R-2), the true Net Indemnity, as corrected,
as of August 15, 2011
and as per the expert report prepared at the request of this honourable Court
by the forensic accountants of Navigant Consulting
was distributed to Class
Members as follows:

CATEGORY

CORRESPONDING

CLASS MEMBERS

CORRESPONDING

AMOUNT

Members who have received and
cashed

a cheque

7424

$1,854,882.14

Members who had a credit applied on
a delivery during the last heating season

4851

Members who were sent a cheque but
never cashed it (more than 1 year)

( ... ) 163

( ... ) $22 140.00

Omitted   customers   who   have
not yet cashed the cheque sent by JEL

5

$158

Members who were sent a cheque less
than 1 year ago but who never cashed it yet

( ... ) $0

( ... ) $0

Members who requested to be sent a
cheque that came back to JEL

42

$8,651.91

Members who couldn't be located
despite all the efforts made

750

$118,701.05

TOTAL

13232

$3,268,195.08

20. It is necessary that
the Court intervene to address this defect in order to avoid undue prejudice to
JEL and the corresponding unjust enrichment to the selected charitable
organizations that would ensue from the status quo;

.

.

.

22. It should finally be
noted that the Petitioner has made verifications of the alleged error in
respect of the Respondent's Records, is satisfied that the request by the
Respondent to have the Court correct the error does not prejudice the members
of the Class, and he therefore does not oppose the Respondent's Motion."

[
9
]

To decide this Motion, the Court was required to
make determinations that related to specialized issues of accounting and
software used in the heating oil industry: determinations which could lead to
substantial reductions in the already-approved "reliquat".
[1]

[
10
]

The Supreme Court of Canada has affirmed the
following statement from Professor Pierre-Claude Lafond in relation to the
Court’s broad discretion under art. 1037 and 1040
C.C.P.
:

"In a class action, the judge has a
different role, as his or her participation continues until the final judgment
is executed. The collective or individual processing of claims and the
distribution
of compensation
constitutes an essential step in the class action and largely
determines the effectiveness of the procedure. The legislature has assigned
responsibility for this to the judge, who turns into a genuine administrator
for purposes of the execution of his or her decision."
[2]

[Court's emphasis]

[
11
]

A similar broad discretion is found in art. 1036

C.C.P.
which applies in this case.

[
12
]

In view of this responsibility, the Court
determined that it required a report from independent forensic accountants to
analyze Joseph Élie Ltée’s assertions. As a result, the independent forensic
accounting firm of Navigant Consulting and specifically forensic accountants
Alain Lajoie, C.A. and Andrea Mathieu, C.A. were engaged to perform this
analysis. Joseph Élie Ltée undertook to pay the costs as well as provide access
to whatever personnel, documents, accounting and computer records would be
necessary for the forensic accountants to undertake this analysis.

[
13
]

Following their work, Mr. Lajoie and Ms. Mathieu
submitted their report to the Court and the parties on August 22, 2011.

[
14
]

The Court conducted a hearing on all Motions for
Rectification on August 29, 2011.

[
15
]

Mr. Labelle, Director of Finances, testified on
behalf of Joseph Élie Ltée. He described how Joseph Élie Ltée, by the terms of
the minutes of settlement, administrated the distribution of the compensation
to its overcharged customers. He indicated that a computer software called
"Minifuel" was essential to administer the distribution of the
compensation. Using data provided by Measurement Canada tests – which showed by
how much each of the tampered-with flow meters over-read the quantity of
delivered fuel oil – Joseph Élie Ltée was able to determine the overcharges for
specific customers who had been serviced by specific delivery trucks equipped
with these misleading flow meters.

[
16
]

He testified that in May to June of 2009, Joseph
Élie Ltée discovered that this computer program was mistakenly encoded and as
such created duplicate delivery transactions.

[
17
]

As a result, Joseph Élie Ltée redid all its
calculations and returned with corrected amounts, which it now wishes be used
to rectify the minutes of settlement and the Rectified Reasons.

[
18
]

In their report, the forensic accountants
confirmed that human error was responsible for the miscalculations. The person
at Joseph Élie Ltée that prepared the final "CD" that was to be filed
into court with all the calculations was not familiar with the data that had
been retrieved, and incorrectly merged different files and included duplicate
transactions that created four types of errors.

[
19
]

Succinctly put, the erroneous final calculations
showed that 60 million litres of fuel oil had been diverted for a total of
13,600 customers when, after verification and correction, in fact 49 million
litres of fuel oil had been diverted for 13,200 customers. Accordingly, the
calculations that the Court had approved on the basis of the original
settlement over-counted by 11 million litres of fuel oil diverted and by 400
customers. In terms of gross volume of heating oil diverted, there was
approximately a 20% difference.

[
20
]

After satisfying itself that the cause of the
error was exactly that as stated by Joseph Élie Ltée,
the forensic accountants carried out the appropriate validation by conducting a
cost efficient sampling to determine whether the suggested corrections were valid.

[
21
]

Based on the evidence the experts gave, the
Court accepts their conclusion that the original Net Indemnity, as approved, of
$4,083,391.00 should in fact have been $3,268.195.00. The Court also confirms
the conclusion by Navigant that
"the global test we performed confirms that Joseph Élie Ltée paid
its customers indemnities which related to the volume that had been
diverted"
. The Court also confirms this
conclusion:
"The
tests that we performed on the "Corrected File" satisfied us in the
sense that we believe that customers who had to be indemnified were properly
indemnified, either by receiving a cheque or a credit note on their account,
Joseph Élie Ltée having made all the necessary efforts to compensate its
customers."

[
22
]

Finally, the forensic accountants were asked to
quantify the "reliquat" based on the corrected calculations.

[
23
]

None of the parties raised any objection to this
analysis. The Court is satisfied – based on the undisputed expertise of these
forensic accountants – that the proper "reliquat" is $149,651.00.

[
24
]

Art. 475
C.C.P.
allows the Court to
correct a judgment in which there is a miscalculation.
[3]
That is the case here.

[
25
]

It is important to underscore that counsel for
the Representative indicated that it was satisfied that this re-rectification
would in no way prejudice any member of the class and that he otherwise had no
objection to the re-rectification. The Court is satisfied that the facts of Joseph Élie Ltée’s request for rectification fall within the Court’s
jurisdiction under art. 475
C.C.P.
The miscalculations – upon which not
only the parties but the Court originally relied – were incorrect through
inadvertence and not the cause of any bad faith.

[
26
]

Accordingly, the amounts for the Total and Net
Indemnity, as well as the "reliquat" contained in the May 28, 2009
Rectified Reasons, approving the settlement and the settlement signed on March
20, 2009, will be rectified for the reasons above-mentioned and for the
additional reasons that will be given below.

[
27
]

To determine the actual
net
"reliquat"
to be distributed in accordance with art. 1036
C.C.P.
, the Court must
now turn to the Fond's Motion which asserts the statutory amount to deduct as
the contribution to the Fonds.

B-       Motion for Rectification by the Fonds

[
28
]

As for the Fonds, it seeks rectification of
paragraph 27 of the Conclusions of the Rectified Reasons also on the grounds of
its own error:  it originally agreed to accept a lesser contribution than that
to which it was statutorily entitled. That paragraph originally said:

"[27]  ORDERS that the Respondent pay
to the Fonds d'aide aux recours collectifs a percentage of 20% up to a maximum
of $20,000.00 from any balance remaining after all of the claims have been paid
out and after the Claim Period has expired;"

[
29
]

These calculations had been agreed to by the
parties and approved in a letter by the Fonds, dated March 30, 2009.

[
30
]

Now, the Fonds takes its Motion for
Rectification on the basis that its entitlement is statutorily determined, is
higher than the agreed-to amount, and cannot be reduced by private agreement.

[
31
]

Counsel both for the Respondent and for Joseph Élie Ltée took no position on this Motion by the Fonds.

[
32
]

The outcome of this Motion has an important
consequence for the Fonds:  under the original agreement, its maximum recovery
from this settlement would be $20,000.00 whereas its statutory entitlement is
$89,790.60.

[
33
]

There is no doubt that the Legislator has
regulated the amount to which the Fonds is entitled
"sur un reliquat ou sur une
réclamation liquidée
"
.
[4]

[
34
]

Where the "reliquat" – as in this case
– is between $100,000.00 and $200,000.00, the Fonds is entitled to 60%. In this
case, 60% of $149,651.00 is $89,790.60.
[5]

[
35
]

The Court of Appeal has confirmed that
regulations once adopted have the force of law: they bind the public administration
and are subject to judicial sanction.
[6]

[
36
]

Elsewhere, the Court of Appeal has also
confirmed the right of the Legislator to allow the Fonds to finance itself from
statute-required deductions from compensation specified (a) in court judgments
or (b) from out of court settlements.
[7]

[
37
]

Since the Legislator has specifically provided
for a percentage amount to be awarded to the Fonds, the Legislator must have
intended that the remainder go to another entity(ies) as determined by the
Courts under art 1036
C.C.P.

[
38
]

As a matter of public order, it is not for the
parties to a settlement (albeit that this was done in good faith) and the Fonds
to agree to any amount other than that statutorily provided for.

[
39
]

Accordingly, this Court determines that the
agreement contemplated by paragraph 27 of the Settlement Agreement is
unenforceable. On the contrary, the amount to which the Fonds is entitled is
the amount of $89,790.60 aforementioned.

[
40
]

Since the Fonds itself also bears responsibility
for creating the problem that necessitated its Motion to Rectify, it is not
appropriate that any costs be awarded on its Motion.

C-        Distribution of the "reliquat"

[
41
]

The final issue is the requirement for the Court
to distribute the "reliquat" of the settlement funds that could not
be otherwise distributed despite reasonable efforts to find and advise all
overcharged customers. Paragraph 29 of the Conclusions of the Rectified Reasons
states:

"[29]  The Court reserves to itself
the jurisdiction once the balance has been determined after all claims have
been paid to request submissions from counsel and potentially from third
parties regarding to what NGO or charitable organization(s) the remainder of
the monies should be paid. In keeping with the jurisprudence, the ultimate
recipients must relate to the interests of the Members of the Group, in some
way;"

[
42
]

The submissions in relation to this paragraph
have been received and the Court must decide who will receive the
"reliquat" remaining from the Total Indemnity that was not able to be
distributed. The Court has determined that amount is: $59,860.40, after the
Fonds receives its statutory contribution of $89,790.60.

[
43
]

The applicable article 1036
C.C.P.

requires:

"The Court disposes of the balance in
the manner it determines, taking particular account of the interest of the
members, after giving the parties and any other persons its designates an
opportunity to be heard."

[
44
]

Under their original settlement (paragraph
5.3.3), the parties agreed that each of them would be allowed to choose which
charity(ies) should receive 50% of the "reliquat". The Court
determined that the Legislator reserved the final determination for the Court
alone, after due consideration of the parties submissions. Those submissions
and one other possibility will now be analyzed to determine the ultimate
disposition of the "reliquat".

[
45
]

Counsel for the Representative submitted to the
Court that 25% of the "reliquat" should be divided equally between
the following four hospitals:

a)

The Montreal Children’s Hospital Foundation;

b)

Fondation CHUM Sainte-Justine;

c)

The Jewish General Hospital Foundation; and

d)

L’Hôpital Notre Dame.

[
46
]

He suggested another 25% should go to the
Respiratory Department of each of those hospitals.

[
47
]

The reasons given by counsel for the
Representative to support these suggestions were:

a)         the vast majority of the class resides in the Greater
Montreal area;

b)         the four hospitals in question are among the most
prominent in Quebec, and likely serve numerous Quebec residents who are members
of the class;

c)         heating oil is a known pollutant, which may present
health risks to those with respiratory problems;

d)         class counsel believes that the vast majority of the
class would be pleased to donate the class portion of the remaining
"reliquat" to hospitals; and

e)         while the present class action was instituted on behalf
of consumers who overpaid, the product for which they overpaid was heating oil,
and class counsel therefore believes that ear-marking the donation to the
Respiratory Department of each hospital properly takes into account the
interest of the members of the class.

[
48
]

Counsel for Joseph Élie Ltée submitted that the
"reliquat" should be distributed to a named local community charity:

a)         on which some of the senior managers of Joseph Élie Ltée
sat on the Board of Directors;

b)         to which the Respondent had made charitable donations in
the past; and

c)         which focussed its charitable activities on a certain
geographic area in Montreal.

[
49
]

Counsel for the Respondent also submitted
"Centraide – The United Way" as an alternative potential recipient.

[
50
]

In reviewing its paragraph 29 of the Conclusions
of the Rectified Reasons, the Court realized that it had inadvertently left out
the word
"Government,"
from the phrase
"
NGO
or charitable organization(s)"
. The Court
rectified this inadvertence of its own motion. As a result, the Court requested
submissions from the parties, the Fonds and if they wished, the Attorney
General of Canada (on behalf of Mesurement Canada) to make any further
submissions they wished under art. 1036
C.C.P.
as regards Measurement
Canada being a potential recipient of the "reliquat".

[
51
]

It was through the original inspections by
Measurement Canada of the delivery trucks that the flow meters of certain
trucks were found to have been illegally tampered with.

[
52
]

Earlier cases have interpreted the phrase
"interest of the members"
in art. 1036
C.C.P.

[
53
]

In a 1990 case
[8]
,
a class action against bailiffs determined that the bailiffs had no right to
use the "Denver boot" to immobilize illegally parked cars. In that
case, the Superior Court found that while a specific charitable organization
devoted to fighting cancer was
"serious, recommended and responsible"
, such an organization did not meet the test of
"interest"
in art. 1036
C.C.P.,
in the context of the facts of that
class action.

[
54
]

In a 1996 case concerning an aborted rock
concert, the Superior Court determined that, since the majority of the members
of the class action were young people,
"interest"

under 1036
C.C.P.
was met where the "reliquat" would be
distributed to organizations that were devoted particularly to young people in
the area of physical and mental health, artistic endeavours, and community
endeavours.
[9]

[
55
]

A 2002 Ontario case
[10]
involved a class action against a
pharmaceutical manufacturer of a drug to treat hypothyroidism. The allegation
was that the manufacturer's advertising was misleading. The proposed class had
approximately 520,000 customers and the settlement was in the neighbourhood of
$2.5 million. Since individual amounts were found too small to be distributed,
the collective distribution of the settlement was for specific research
projects, education and outreach having to do with thyroid disease. In this
Court’s opinion, this decision is also an instructive example of the
"interest"
of class members, albeit not binding on this Court.

[
56
]

Article 1036
C.C.P.
provides the Court
with a large judicial discretion to consider
"particularly the interests of the members of the
group"
.

[
57
]

The "reliquat" under art. 1036
C.C.P.

may arise in at least two situations:

a)

where the total indemnity is to be distributed
to other than the members, since the amount involved is so small or the
difficulty in determining the identity of the members so great (art. 1034
C.C.P.
);
or

b)

where there has already been an individual
distribution and a remainder is left because either certain claims have been
rejected or certain members cannot be found. This is the present case.

[
58
]

Here, the "reliquat" actually consists
of those funds from the settlement that were intended to
compensate

certain members for their overpayments but ultimately, these members could not
be found.

[
59
]

Amongst the various definitions that the word
"interest"
may have, the Court believes that the following two definitions are
the most appropriate:

a)

the first is drawn from
Le Petit Robert 2012
[11]
:
"
Avantage (cf) y trouver son compte
"
; and

b)

from the
Concise Oxford Dictionary of Current
English, 9
th
Edition
[12]
:

"interest"
"Advantage
or profit, especially when financial

(i.e. it is in your interest to go; look
after your own interest)
"
.

[
60
]

The Court of Appeal has already said that the
execution of the judgment in a class action must
"be at the same time practical and
rational
"

[this Court's
emphasis].
[13]

[
61
]

In the present case, it is not in the interest
of the members compensated that the "reliquat" be returned to Joseph
Élie Ltée. At the same time, it would not be in the interest of the members
that the "reliquat" be divided up between those members who have been
found and have already been compensated.

[
62
]

Furthermore, there is no evidence in the Court
record that heating oil does present a health risk from pollution, or that the
members of the class are specifically affected by respiratory problems. While
the Court respects the good intentions of both parties in making their
suggestions, the fact is that whether they be hospitals, hospital respiratory
departments, goodwill organizations or the United Way, none of these potential
recipients have a direct enough
"interest"
for the members on
the particular facts of this case, where the "mischief" at issue is
the fraudulent tampering with fuel oil flow meters.

[
63
]

According to Professor Pierre-Claude Lafond
[14]
, he notes in relation to art. 1036
C.C.P.
:

"Il importe par dessus tout de se
rappeler la fonction compensatoire du recours collectif et la correspondance
qui doit exister entre la victime du préjudice subi et le bénéficiaire de
l'indemnisation. Si cette compensation ne peut procéder de manière directe, le
tribunal doit intervenir pour que l'objectif soit atteint indirectement."

[
64
]

In her comparative text on common law class
actions, Professor Rachael P. Mulheron
[15]

notes:

"Indeed, both Ontario and British
Columbia statutes permit the court to make a cy-pres distribution as the first
option in respect of any portion of an aggregate award that cannot be
distributed directly to individual class members."

[
65
]

In Ontario, the specific statute is art. 26 (4)
of the
Class Proceedings Act
[16]

("the
Act
") which notes:

"The Court may order that all or a
part of an award under s. 24 that has not been distributed within the time set
by the court be applied in any manner
that may reasonably be expected to
benefit class members
, even though it does not provide for monetary relief
to individual class members, if the court is satisfied that a reasonable number
of class members who would not otherwise receive relief would benefit from the
order."
[this
Court's emphasis]

[
66
]

At art. 26 (6) of the
Act
specifically
provides for a distribution under art. 26 (4) to persons
who are not class members or persons who may otherwise receive monetary relief
as a result of the class proceeding.

[
67
]

The Legislator has clearly provided the Court
with a very broad discretion, while specifically emphasizing that the
distribution be related to the "members' interests" Some greater
precision as to what the Legislator intended would be helpful to both the Court
and counsel. However in light of the present general wording, the Court must
ask itself what distribution and to whom would reasonably meet this test.

[
68
]

Based on the above, and with the greatest of
respect to the excellent work done by the charitable and hospital institutions
suggested, the Court is satisfied that they are not covered by the application
of art. 1036
C.C.P.
to the facts of this case. On the other hand, the
Court is satisfied that Measurement Canada – irrespective of its status a
federal–government organization – is the type of recipient intended by the
present wording of art. 1036 because of the following rational connections with
this case.

[
69
]

Had it not been for the inspectors of
Measurement Canada, the illegal tampering with the fuel oil flow meters on the
delivery trucks would likely never have been discovered. The investigative work
of such inspectors, and the knowledge by heating oil truck operators that such
inspectors do inspect, is a powerful dissuasion to the dishonest tactics seen
by the third party delivery companies in the present file. The dissuasion,
prevention and discovery of such dishonest tactics is in the interest of all
home heating oil consumers, including particularly those that have been
overcharged in the present case.

[
70
]

Counsel for the Attorney General of Canada
advised the Court that only the Parliament of Canada could allocate funds to
federal government departments. Recognizing this fundamental division of
powers, the Court nonetheless believes that the intention of this distribution
– as extra not replacement operational funding – will be respected.

[
71
]

Measurement Canada requires funds to carry out
its operations. Irrespective of the size of the amount, this amount is a
contribution which assists in making these inspections possible, including the
ability to pay for greater publicity in the marketplace to publicize the
existence of such inspections and the applicable penalties to dissuade future
wrongdoing.

[
72
]

For these reasons, Joseph
Élie Ltée will be directed to pay the "reliquat" to the Federal
Government with the specific recommendation that these funds be attributed
in
addition
to those already budgeted for the operation of the fuel oil inspection
section of Measurement Canada in the Greater Montreal
area.

[
73
]

In conclusion, the Court expresses its
appreciation for the professionalism and rigour exercised by all counsel
involved in this file.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
74
]

RECTIFIES
the
judgment rendered on May 28, 2009 authorizing the class action solely for the
purpose of a settlement and approving the Settlement Agreement signed by the
parties on March 20, 2009, in order:

a)        that the Total Indemnity as defined in the said Agreement

RECTIFIED REASONS FOR
JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[1-A]  In view of the Rectification of
Judgment of May 29, 2009 for reasons of inadvertence, the Conclusions have
been rectified.

[1]

The Court is seized with a "Motion to
Approve a Class Action Settlement Agreement and Transaction, and to Approve the
Payment of Legal Fees by the Class" (the "Motion"). Unless
otherwise defined herein, the same defined terms will be used as in the Motion
and the
Settlement Agreement
.

[2]

The original "Motion for Authorization to
Institute a Class Action and to Obtain the Status of Representative" was
taken by the Applicant on January 21, 2008.

[3]

The relevant facts are as follows. Government
authorities found that two independent contractors that were hired by the
Respondent to deliver heating oil to its customers had tempered with the
measuring meters on their delivery trucks so as to divert heating oil charged
to the customers (the "diversion") during the period from January 5,
2006 to March 27, 2007 (the "Period").

[4]

Specific trucks from these two contractors were
found to have had their meters tampered with. Measurement Canada performed three tests on each of the
suspect delivery trucks in order to determine the percentage degree of error of
the tampered meters that had been involved in the diversion during the Period.

[5]

The results of the Measurement Canada Tests were
filed into Court.
[i]

[6]

For settlement purposes, the Respondent compiled
records of every delivery made by each of these trucks during the Period (the
"Records"). These Records indicate, amongst other things, the date of
each delivery, the truck that made the delivery, the volume of heating oil that
was to have been delivered for each delivery and the price charged by the
Respondent for the volume of heating oil that was alleged to have been
delivered for each delivery, plus taxes.

[7]

The quantum of the
Settlement Agreement

was essentially worked out as follows. The total amount paid for each of the
Respondent's clients during the Period was established. This was done by
computer program. A representative example using the Applicant as a case in
point was provided to the Court.
[ii]

[8]

The Measurement Canada Tests essentially showed
three slightly different test results for each of the trucks. The parties
agreed to take the highest percentage diversion found by Measurement Canada and
then apply this to the actual deliveries to arrive at an amount that would be a
close approximation of the actual loss suffered by each customer as a result of
the diversion.

[9]

Using this method, it was calculated that the
customers paid collectively a maximum of $4,461,046.68 for heating oil that was
probably diverted during the Period.

[10]

Under the
Settlement Agreement
, the
Respondent will reimburse to the Members of the Group, collectively, the sum of
$4,461,046.68, representing the maximum amount that the Respondent's customers
likely paid for heating oil that was not delivered during the Period, inclusive
of taxes, based on the Measurement Canada Tests and the Records (the
"Total Indemnity").

[11]

On Wednesday, March 18, 2009, a "Notice of
Proposed Settlement" which gave the date of the approval hearing of April
2, 2009 was published in English in the Montreal Gazette and in French in  La Presse. The Court determines that the notices met
all legal requirements.

[12]

Thereafter, the approval hearing was held on
April 2, 2009 when the Court received representations from counsel for both
parties. No one else came forward to make other representations.

[13]

The role of the Court at this stage requires a
three step analysis:

1-         the determination by the Court that the criteria of art.
1003,
C.C.P.
have been met so that the Court can authorize the bringing
of the class action and ascribing the status of representative to the
Petitioner for the purposes of considering the settlement;

2-         the determination of whether the proposed
Settlement
Agreement
should be accepted; and

3-         the demand to approve the legal fees and disbursements of
Class Counsel.

A-        AUTHORIZATION
OF THE CLASS ACTION

[14]

The Court will now consider whether this
proceeding meets the four tests of art. 1003 (a)-(d),
C.C.P.
The
headings will be the actual wording of each of those sub-sections.

a)        The Recourses of the Members Raise Identical, Similar or
Related Questions of Law or Fact

[15]

The identical, similar or related questions of
fact

to be decided for all Members of the Group are:

a)         whether and how much money the Respondent was paid by the
Members of the Group collectively for heating oil not delivered;

b)         over what period of time; and

c)         whether the Respondent was at fault in not verifying
whether its independent contractors could and did temper with the measurement
meters on their delivery trucks.

[16]

Identical, similar or related questions of
law

to be decided on the merits for all Members of the Group include:

a)         whether the Respondent is liable to compensate its
customers for money they have overpaid for heating oil that was not delivered;
and

b)         whether this sale is covered by the
Consumer
Protection Act
("
C.P.A.
") and if so, whether punitive
damages may be claimed pursuant to the
C.P.A.

[17]

The main question that must be dealt with
individually is the amount that each Member of the Group is entitled to recover
from the amount of damages that the Respondent may be required to pay
collectively.

[18]

In view of the similarity of the questions of
fact and law involved in this proceeding, the Court determines that this first
criterion has been met.

b)        The Facts Alleged Seem to Justify the
Conclusions Sought

[19]

Without needing to characterize whether the
contract falls under the
C.P.A.
or not, the fact remains that if the
Petitioner is able to prove the allegations made, the Members of the Group
would be entitled to collect certain compensatory damages on the basis of the
Respondent's fault.

[20]

Accordingly, the Court finds that the second
criterion is met.

c)         The Composition of the Group Makes the Application of
Art. 59 or
67, C
.C.P. Difficult or Impracticable

[21]

A review of Exhibit R-7, a partial list of the
Respondent's customers during the Period, shows the large number of individuals
involved. Clearly, only the Respondent possesses the exact details of all the
Members of the Group's names, whereabouts and transactions.

[22]

Given the amounts in issue as shown by Exhibit
R-7, it is clear that the wrongs alleged by the Petitioner would, although
important, not make it worthwhile for each of the customers to sue
individually. Examples of such amounts are:  $41.00 and $24.70.

[23]

These figures demonstrate just how useful and
necessary the class action is in such circumstances.

[24]

On this basis, this third criterion is met.

d)        The Member to Who the Court Intends to Ascribe the Status
of Representative is in a Position to Represent the Members Adequately

[25]

The Court is satisfied that the Petitioner is
particularly well-qualified for this purpose. In addition to being a customer
of the Respondent, he is retired and has had the time to devote to the case. He
also has experience and expertise in the heating oil industry, having held a
senior position at another Montreal heating oil company for many years. He attended with Class Counsel
at numerous court appearances.

[26]

Accordingly, the Court determines that the
fourth criterion is met.

[27]

Therefore, the Court is satisfied that all four
criteria of art. 1003,
C
.C.P.
have been met.

B-        APPROVING THE SETTLEMENT

[28]

The original proceeding was undertaken on
January 21, 2008 and the
Settlement Agreement
was signed on March 20,
2009.

[29]

The criteria that the Court must apply to
approve a settlement in class action matters are well-known.
[iii]

[30]

The Court determines that the most important
criteria for the facts of this case are:

a)         the nature of the evidence available;

b)         the levels of compensation for the victims and the means
of reaching those victims;

c)

the terms and conditions of the settlement; and

d)

the absence of any objections to the settlement.

[31]

The evidence filed in the Court from Measurement
Canada
[iv]
notes
clearly the percentage of oil delivered that was under-calculated by the oil
measurement meters.

[32]

The fact that the independent contractors
pleaded guilty in Court to the diversion is convincing evidence that the
diversion took place. It is important to underscore that there is no proof
whatsoever before this Court linking the Respondent in any way to the
misfeasance committed by the independent contractors.

[33]

The Court is satisfied that the methodology for
calculating the damages provides the victims with an exceptional recovery of
almost the full value of the probable loss they suffered.

[34]

Moreover, the cooperation of the Respondent with
the Petitioner to providing the computer printout for all customers showing the
highest probable value of their loss is extremely helpful to ensure that Class
Counsel:

i-

knows the names of all Members of the Group; and

ii-

knows their addresses and can see the
calculations showing the highest probable loss they would have suffered which
collectively is only 7.5% less than the full amount that has been agreed to be
paid by the Respondent. Furthermore, the Respondent has undertaken to contact
each of those customers directly and provide the option of either receiving the
full amount of the Individual Indemnity by cheque or by receiving an equivalent
credit on future oil delivery. This approach will be followed with those
clients that suffered a loss during the Period and have remained customers to
this day or have agreed to return as customers of the Respondent.

[35]

For those customers during the Period who
suffered losses and who do not wish to be customers of the Respondent, these
individuals will be provided with a cheque in payment for the loss.

[36]

The Respondent has undertaken to do all of this
work itself thereby eliminating additional costs of administration.

[37]

For those clients which suffered losses but who
can no longer be traced, they will be provided with a special notice, in both
the Montreal newspapers
previously involved, of their right to make a claim within the Claim Period.
Any balance that remains after such claims have been paid will be put into an
account and dealt with under art. 1036,
C.C.P.

[38]

The final advantage of this settlement is that
compensation will be received by the Members of the Group without them having
to take any positive action even as far as making a claim is concerned. The
Respondent will communicate with each Member of the Group who is still a client
by way of a letter which has been approved by the Court.

[39]

The Respondent will contact the Inactive
Accounts (those accounts that have become inactive between January 5, 2006 and
the date of this judgment) and the Respondent will contact those persons
individually by telephone to invite them to become a customer of the Respondent
once again. A letter following up on the telephone call will be sent advising
them of the amounts they are entitled to pursuant to the
Settlement
Agreement
. Those Inactive Accounts who decide to become customers shall be
paid their Individual Indemnity in the form of credits in the same way as the
active accounts unless they request in writing to receive a cheque. Those
Inactive Accounts who chose not to become customers of the Respondent, again,
shall be paid their Individual Indemnity by cheque.

[40]

The Respondent shall regularly provide Class
Counsel with a CD Rom containing the updated Records to include a column which
indicates those Members of the Group entitled to reimbursement and who have
received their Individual Indemnity and those who have not. Class Counsel will
perform spot checks to ensure that the Members of the Group entitled to
reimbursement have received their Individual Indemnity.

[41]

The Court will retain jurisdiction – which the
parties have also agreed to – to resolve any issues regarding the
interpretation of the
Settlement Agreement
, to ensure that all payments
are properly made, and as required, to interpret and enforce the terms,
conditions and obligations arising under the
Settlement Agreement
.

[42]

The Court is satisfied for the reasons
above-noted that the
Settlement Agreement
is just, equitable, reasonable
and in the best interest of the Group. An overview of the Court's reasons are:

a)         the Total Indemnity provides for almost full
recovery for all victims;

b)

the Respondent is paying all the costs of
administration and it is far from clear that even if this matter went to trial
that the Members of the Group would be likely to obtain any more than they
would through this settlement, all the while achieving the substantial saving
of legal fees achieved through a settlement; and

c)

the Respondent does not require that any
undisbursed balance be returned to it.

[43]

Had this matter gone to trial, a major debate
would have been whether the Respondent committed a fault by not knowing or not
investigating earlier the actions of these two independent contractors. The
Settlement
Agreement
specifically notes that the Respondent makes no admission of
liability in this area.

[44]

That said, the Respondent has acted as a
responsible corporate citizen in indemnifying its customers in circumstances
where it never received any economic benefit from the illegal acts of its
independent contractors but, on the contrary, is paying for the consequences of
those illegal acts through the
Settlement Agreement
. Counsel for the
Respondent indicated that the Respondent was a victim in this process.

C-        THE LEGAL FEES

[45]

The Petitioner signed a "Mandate and Fee
Agreement" dated January 21, 2008
[v]
in
which he agreed to pay 20% of the value of any amounts received prior to a
judgment authorizing a class action.

[46]

Class Counsel have been able to negotiate that
the Respondent pays 12.5% of the Total Indemnity (plus applicable taxes) on
account of Class Counsel fees, disbursements and costs in addition to the Total
Indemnity. Accordingly, only 7.5% of the Total Indemnity (plus applicable
taxes) are to be paid on behalf of the Members of the Group to Class Counsel
for their legal services.

[47]

This amount of 7.5% of the Total Indemnity comes
to $334,578.50 without taxes and $377,655.49 with taxes.
[vi]

[48]

Contingency fees are well-known in the Province of Québec
as is the principle of
quantum meruit
,

wherein the amount of
legal fees to be paid is based, amongst other things, upon the complexity of
the file and the result obtained.

[49]

It must be remembered that the Total Indemnity
in this case is very close to 100% which is only reduced by the 7.5% of legal
fees above-mentioned. This recovery is proportionate to the costs negotiated
between the parties and for this reason will be approved.

CONCLUSION

[50]

For practical reasons, the conclusions of the
judgment will be rendered under separate cover but will reflect these reasons.
